🌳 Two more choices, drawn or decided in their owner notes

notes.html:
What your code puts in the window on each request, in what order, and what it removes. Note 44 names the layer; 45 sets how much each part may use; 46, 47 and 54 say where things go and how much is too much; 48 and 49 say what it costs and how order decides that; 50, 51 and 52 say what to take out; 53 handles turns that depend on earlier turns. Read each arrow as a sentence: the budget is spent by position in lost in the middle.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING. Notes 47 and 54 share one node.

The window is over budget: what goes first?

  • Cap at the source (45): if the oversized part is a session document the user needs whole, the cap doesn't apply; go down the tree.
  • 🧹 Clear tool results (51): if the agent must re-read a raw payload later, keep a handle it can re-fetch.
  • Structured summary (50): if each turn stands alone, as in simple support chat, dropping is cheaper and has no hidden error.
  • Extract or prune (50): if the text is code, numbers or legal wording, extract whole spans; never prune tokens.
  • 🪟 Drop the middle (51): if a prompt cache is in use, do it rarely and in one large step.

Two more choices, drawn or decided in their owner notes

  • Put the whole document in, or retrieve from it? (54). Would retrieval of a few chunks do? Yes for fact lookup with a source. Put the whole thing in when the answer is a property of the whole document and it sits below the length where your own sweep shows accuracy falling.
  • Is caching worth turning on for this route? (49). Would no caching do? Yes if a prefix is used once, or less often than the cache lifetime. Otherwise the break-even is reached on the second or third request.

notes.title: Context Engineering vs Prompt Engineering — Writing the String vs Deciding What Fills the Window
notes.html:
References

Anthropic Engineering: effective context engineering for AI agents · Chroma 2025: Context Rot · Anthropic: context windows · Prompting Guide: context engineering guide

TL;DR

Prompt engineering writes a string, once, at design time. Context engineering designs the code that fills the window on every request, and decides what leaves when it doesn't fit. The scarce thing is not window size. It is how well the model uses what is there. Both layers exist at once: the system prompt inside the window is still an authored string.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchdesign time
Flow:authored system prompt + tool definitionshistory so farretrieved texttool resultsbudget and eviction policythe window for this callmodelits output joins the history

Recall

Prompt Answer
The one-line difference? One authors a string; the other decides what enters the window each call.
What forced the new name? Agent and tool loops: the window became something code builds and that grows.
The test for which one you're doing? "What is in the window on turn 15, and who decided?"

The idea

An agent's system prompt is carefully written and well tested. On turn 15 of a real session it gives a poor answer. Nobody wrote turn 15's context: it is the system prompt plus whatever fourteen tool calls left behind, including two failed attempts and a 9,000-token API response from turn three. The prompt was fine. What surrounded it was not.

In a single call, a person decides everything the model sees. In a loop, your code decides, request by request: what to keep from earlier turns, how much retrieved text to add, what to drop when space runs out. That code is a component with its own logic, its own failures and its own tests. Calling it context engineering is just giving the component a name.

Ask a team: "what exactly is in the window on turn 15, and who decided?" If the answer is a template file, they are doing prompt engineering. If the answer is a budget, an eviction rule and a compaction trigger, they are doing context engineering, and those are the parts that now break.

Unlike a sentence in a prompt, an assembly rule is code: it is enforced, every time.

The trade: an assembly layer gives control over what the model sees on long runs, and is one more component to build and test. A single fixed-shape call doesn't need it.

How it works

The same request, seen as two layers.

Prompt engineering Context engineering
What you produce a template string an assembly policy and a budget
Decided when design time, by a person request time, by code
Optimises how clear the instruction is what occupies the window, and what leaves
Fails as ambiguity, format drift pollution, the needed fact evicted, a cache that never hits
Tested by a golden set a golden set plus hit rate, budget use and results by turn depth

Every other note in this section is one policy inside that assembly step: how much, where, in what order for the cache, what to keep of the history, how to shrink it.

Evolution

Lineage:2020–22 one authored prompt per call2023 retrieval fills one slot of a template2024 agent loops make the window grow by itselfmid-2025 "context engineering" namedSep 2025 onward providers ship server-side context management
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): the term is settled; the tooling (compaction, context editing) is still in beta at the provider read for this note.
  • Stronger-model test: no. Longer windows remove hard overflow, and the provider's own documentation says accuracy and recall degrade as token count grows. What won't change: something must decide what the model sees, and on a long run that something is code.

Measure it

  • Offline: the same golden set scored by turn depth (turn 1, 10, 30), against the system with no eviction. An assembly change should hold or raise the deep-turn score.
  • In production: tokens per region per request, what was evicted, cache-read share, and quality by turn depth. A flat average with a falling deep-turn score is the signal.
  • Enforced by: the assembly code: budgets, order and eviction always run. Whether the model uses what it was given well is not enforced by anything.

Interview

30-second answer: Prompt engineering is authoring a string. Context engineering is designing the system that assembles the window at call time, the system prompt, tools, retrieved chunks, history and tool outputs, and decides what's evicted. The shift came from agents, where the window grows on its own. It matters because the scarce resource is the model's use of the window, which degrades with length well inside the advertised limit.

Q · Mechanism — Isn't this a rebrand? Prompts always had retrieved text in them. Partly, and I'd say so. One thing did change: ownership of the window moved from a person at design time to code at request time. In a classic retrieval call a person wrote the template and a retriever filled one slot. In an agent loop nobody authors the fifteenth turn; it's what earlier tool calls left plus what the compaction rule kept. That is a component with logic and failure modes, and it wasn't one before.

Q · Trade-off — Windows are huge now. Why not put everything in? The simpler rung is exactly that, and for a short, bounded task it is fine. Beyond that, window size is capacity, not quality: accuracy declines with input length, and related-but-wrong content actively misleads. There's also arithmetic. Every extra token is paid on every call, slows the first token, and a large changing context defeats the cache. So I use the headroom as a safety margin and curate for relevance. The measurements are in long-context prompting.

Pitfalls

  • "Context engineering is what we call prompt engineering now"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the new term arrived as the old one went out of fashion.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: they are two layers and both remain. The system prompt is authored text; assembly governs what sits around it on turn fifteen.
    ↳ Think instead: an excellent prompt in a polluted window still fails; diagnose which layer broke.
  • "A bigger window makes the context problem go away"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: overflow errors do disappear.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the problem moves from truncation, which is loud, to slightly worse answers on long sessions, which is silent and falls on the cases nobody evaluated.
    ↳ Think instead: a bigger window trades a visible error for an invisible one.
  • Not the same: context engineering here vs in an agent loop
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the same four words are used for both.
    ↳ Difference: this section covers the window of one conversation: budget, order, cache, history. Strategies across an agent's run (writing to a scratchpad, isolating work in sub-agents) belong to the Agentic note.
    ↳ Think instead: window policy here; loop strategy there.
  • Don't build the machinery before you have the failure.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: budgets, eviction and compaction sound like table stakes.
    ↳ What goes wrong: each is a component that can itself drop the needed fact, and a one-call task never needed any of them.
    ↳ Do instead: ship the template, measure where it breaks by turn depth, add the one policy that fixes that.
  • Shelf life: the two layers are durable. The name, and how much of the assembly the provider does for you, are moving.

Connections

  • Owned elsewhere: context engineering (Agentic) covers the loop strategies; the vocabulary map places the terms.
  • Measured by component vs end-to-end eval: separating a prompt failure from an assembly failure.
  • Drilled in context engineering, not prompting.

notes.title: Context Window Budgeting — A Subtraction in Priority Order
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: context windows · Hsieh et al. 2024: RULER · Chroma 2025: Context Rot · Anthropic Engineering: effective context engineering for AI agents · Anthropic: context editing

TL;DR

Everything shares one window: system prompt, tool definitions, history, retrieved text, tool results and the answer about to be written. Budgeting decides beforehand how much each may take. It is a subtraction in priority order, not a percentage split: reserve the output, subtract the fixed parts, then let the changing parts claim what is left by priority. Budget against the length your task works at, not the advertised one, and count tokens; don't estimate them.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:working lengthminus output reserveminus system + toolsworking budgetfill by priority: goal, recent turns, retrieved text, old tool resultscap, clear, compress, or refuse loudly

Recall

Prompt Answer
What is reserved first? The output: input and output share the window.
The fixed floor? System prompt plus tool definitions, present on every call.
Which parts grow without bound? Tool results, then history. Retrieval is bounded by your k.
Budget against which length? The length your own eval holds up at, below the advertised window.
Why not truncate the oldest? The oldest message is usually the user's goal.
Draw by hand: the window as a column Output reserve, system, tools, pinned goal, recent turns, retrieved text, old tool results; cuts start from the bottom.

The idea

A support agent works in testing and fails for one customer. Their account lookup returns 30,000 rows where the test account returned three. The tool result fills the window, the framework quietly trims the oldest messages to make room, and the first message, where the customer said what they wanted, is gone. The agent answers a question nobody asked.

Two mistakes. Nothing limited what a single tool could return, so one part of the window was sized by its average and broke at its peak. And when space ran out, the rule for what to drop was "oldest first", which is a rule about time, not about importance.

A budget fixes both. Before the call, each part of the window has a cap. The tool result is cut at the tool, with a note saying it was cut. When the total is still too large, parts are dropped in order of how little they matter now: old raw tool results first, the user's goal never.

This is code, so it holds on every request. That is the difference between a budget and a sentence in the prompt asking the model to "be brief with context".

The trade: a budgeter is a component to build and it can evict something that mattered; without one, the same eviction happens anyway, by accident and in the wrong order.

How it works

The window for one request, top to bottom, with what each part is allowed.

Region Tokens Changes every Cut order
Output reserve (max_tokens) fixed, set first never never: reserved before anything else
System prompt fixed deploy never
Tool definitions fixed deploy never; shrink at deploy time if too large
Pinned goal and stated constraints small session never
Recent turns, verbatim floor of the last few turn last
Retrieved text k × chunk size request third: rerank down to a smaller k
Middle history grows turn second: summarise or drop
Old raw tool results unbounded unless capped turn first

The numbers come from one subtraction.

budget  = L_work − T_out − H            ← working length, minus output reserve, minus headroom for counting error
work    = budget − T_sys − T_tools      ← what is left for everything that changes
fill    : by priority until work is used ← spare room flows to whoever needs it; no fixed shares

L_work is the term people skip. It is the input length at which your own eval still holds, and it is usually well below the advertised window.

Rule What actually happens
Cap at the source A tool truncates its own output and says so, before the result reaches the assembler. After that point every option is worse.
Budget the peak Size each part by its 99th percentile. The request that overflows is the one where a "constant" part was a distribution.
Count, don't estimate Characters ÷ 4 is roughly right for English prose and badly wrong for JSON, code, other scripts and images. Use the provider's tokeniser or counting endpoint.
Fail loudly If the floor alone exceeds the budget, that is a deploy error. A refused request can be retried differently; a silently shortened one cannot.

How much the retrieved-text row should get is owned by the RAG note on context window budgeting; the ways to shrink a row are in context compression.

Evolution

Lineage:2020–22 small windows: budgeting to avoid a hard error2023 windows of 100k and moreApr 2024 RULER: usable length is below advertised lengthJul 2025 decay with length measured on current models2025–26 million-token windows; providers offer server-side clearing
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026).
  • Stronger-model test: no. Larger windows remove the overflow error and leave cost, latency and decay with length. What won't change: output and input share one space, and something has to decide what is dropped.
  • Checked on: window sizes and overflow behaviour differ by provider and model; the dated values are in the chapter map's Landscape table.

Code

A priority-ordered assembler. The model is never asked to manage its own window.

def assemble(parts, L_work, max_tokens, count, headroom=1000):
    budget = L_work - max_tokens - headroom               # ① output shares the window: reserve it first
    floor = count(parts.system) + count(parts.tools)      # ② the fixed parts
    if floor > budget:
        raise ConfigError(floor)                          # a deploy-time bug, not a runtime surprise
    work, kept, used = budget - floor, [], 0
    for p in sorted(parts.changing, key=lambda p: p.priority):   # ③ goal, recent turns, retrieved, old tools
        n = count(p)
        if used + n <= work:
            kept.append(p); used += n
        elif p.summary and used + count(p.summary) <= work:
            kept.append(p.summary); used += count(p.summary)     # cheaper than losing it
        else:
            metrics.incr("ctx.evicted", kind=p.kind)             # ④ count what you drop
    metrics.gauge("ctx.used", (floor + used) / budget)           # alert on the p99 of this
    return parts.system, parts.tools, kept

Break it: the belief that dropping the oldest messages is a safe default.

history = [("goal", "refund order 8841, do not cancel the subscription")] + [("tool", "x" * 500)] * 6 + [("user", "ok go ahead")]
def trim_oldest(msgs, limit):                      # what many framework defaults do
    while sum(len(t) for _, t in msgs) > limit: msgs = msgs[1:]
    return msgs
def by_priority(msgs, limit):                      # drop raw tool results first, never the goal
    msgs = list(msgs)
    while sum(len(t) for _, t in msgs) > limit: msgs.remove(next(m for m in msgs if m[0] == "tool"))
    return msgs
print([k for k, _ in trim_oldest(history, 1600)], [k for k, _ in by_priority(history, 1600)])
# look for: "goal" missing from the first list and present in the second
# naive belief predicts: both keep what matters

Run on Python 3.9, it prints ['tool', 'tool', 'tool', 'user'] and ['goal', 'tool', 'tool', 'tool', 'user']. Same limit, same history: the first agent no longer knows it must not cancel the subscription.

Measure it

  • Offline: task success by turn depth on long-session fixtures, against the unbudgeted system. An eviction change that saves tokens and lowers the turn-30 score should not ship.
  • In production: window use as a share of the budget (alert on the p99, not on overflow errors), evictions by kind, and the largest tool result per tool.
  • Enforced by: the assembler and the per-tool output cap. Both are code and run on every request.

Interview

30-second answer: Budgeting is deciding ahead of time how many tokens each part of the window gets. I reserve the output first, because input and output share the window; then the fixed floor of system prompt and tool schemas; what remains is split by priority between retrieved text, history and tool results. I enforce it with a counting assembler, and I budget against the length my eval holds up at, not the advertised window.

Q · Mechanism — Walk me through the arithmetic. Start from the working length and subtract in order. First the output reserve, because a long answer and a long input compete for one space. Then the fixed floor: system prompt and tool definitions, which for an agent with a dozen tools is thousands of tokens before any user content. What's left is the working budget. Retrieval is bounded by k times chunk size. History grows with turns. Tool results grow with whatever a tool returns. So it's a priority order with floors, not fixed shares.

Q · Trade-off — You're 20% over on a long conversation. What goes first? The simpler rung is to check whether a per-tool cap and a smaller k remove the problem without any eviction. If not, I cut by information per token: old raw tool results first, because the model already wrote down what mattered. Then the middle of the history becomes a summary while recent turns stay verbatim. Retrieved text is cut by reranking to fewer chunks, not by slicing. I never cut the system prompt, the tool definitions or the user's original goal.

Q · Failure — The budget holds for 95% of requests and blows up on the rest. A part budgeted as a constant is a distribution. Usually a tool: three rows in testing, thirty thousand for one customer. Second, token estimates from character counts, which are far off for JSON, code and non-Latin scripts. Third, images. I'd confirm from per-part token counts on the failing requests. The fix is one pattern: count for real, cap each part at its source, and alert on budget use at the 99th percentile.

Q · Design — A multi-tenant agent platform where tenants bring their own tools and documents. Tenants can't be trusted to bound their own parts, so the budget is a platform policy checked at deploy: a tenant whose system prompt exceeds the floor cap fails their deploy, not their users' requests. An assembler sits between every agent and the model, counts every part and emits a receipt of what was kept and dropped. Oversized tool results are capped at a tool proxy and replaced by a handle. I'd watch quality by turn depth first. The layers are in the prompt-layer reference architecture.

Pitfalls

  • "The context window is the input limit"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it is described as how much the model can read.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it is the limit on input plus output together, including any thinking tokens. A request that fits can still run out of room while answering.
    ↳ Think instead: reserve the output first; what is left is the input budget.
  • "If it fits, it's fine"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: no error means success in most systems.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: accuracy falls as input grows, and related-but-wrong content misleads. A window at 90% can answer worse than the same question at 20%.
    ↳ Think instead: fitting is the minimum; the budget is set by where quality holds.
  • "Truncating the oldest messages is a safe default"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: frameworks do it, and old usually does mean less relevant.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the oldest message is usually the goal. Agents that forget what they were doing around turn twenty are mostly agents whose trimmer ate turn one.
    ↳ Think instead: order of arrival is not order of importance; pin the goal.
  • Not the same: advertised length vs working length
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: only one of them is on the model card.
    ↳ Difference: the advertised length is what the API accepts. The working length is where your task's accuracy still holds, found by a sweep on your own data.
    ↳ Think instead: budget to the number you measured.
  • Don't split the budget by fixed percentages.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "40% retrieval, 40% history, 20% tools" is easy to explain.
    ↳ What goes wrong: when one part is empty its share is wasted while another part is being cut.
    ↳ Do instead: floors for what must survive, then a priority order for the rest.
  • Don't build eviction before you have measured use.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a compaction pipeline feels like responsible engineering.
    ↳ What goes wrong: at a 99th-percentile use of 30% it only adds a way to lose facts.
    ↳ Do instead: cap tool outputs first; that one change removes most overflows.
  • Shelf life: the subtraction and the priority order are durable. Window sizes, overflow behaviour and what the provider will clear for you are volatile.

Connections

  • Owned elsewhere: context window budgeting (RAG) sizes the retrieved-text share; context utilization (LLM-Production) covers how working length is benchmarked.
  • Used by ordering for the cache: eviction rewrites the prefix, so the two are designed together.
  • Measured by long-context prompting: the sweep that finds L_work.
  • Costed in cost modelling: tokens per region become money.
  • Drilled in budget a 128k window.

notes.title: Lost in the Middle — Being in the Window Is Not Being Used
notes.html:
References

Liu et al. 2023: Lost in the Middle · Hsieh et al. 2024: RULER · Chroma 2025: Context Rot · Modarressi et al. 2025: NoLiMa · Anthropic: prompting best practices

TL;DR

A model does not use a long input evenly. Content at the start and the end is used best; content in the middle is used worst: a U-shaped curve. So the right passage can be present and still ignored: retrieval recall stops predicting answer accuracy. The best fix is to send less. The cheap fix is to put the best material at the two ends and the question last.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:10 retrieved chunksrerankkeep 4best first, second-best lastquestion at the endask for the supporting quote firstcheck the quote exists

Recall

Prompt Answer
Shape of the curve? U: best at the start and end, worst in the middle.
What was varied in the 2023 study? Only the position of the answer-bearing document.
Does a long-context model fix it? No. The study found it in extended-context models too.
Best mitigation? Fewer, better chunks: a small input has almost no middle.
What can reordering not fix? Distractors, and answers that need an inference step.
Draw by hand: the curve Accuracy against position: high at the left, a dip in the middle, high again at the right.

The idea

A contract Q&A system retrieves ten chunks per question. Offline, the chunk containing the answer is almost always among the ten. Users still get wrong answers far more often than that. The team tunes the retriever for a month and nothing improves.

The retriever was fine. Log where the answer-bearing chunk landed among the ten and compare with whether the answer was right: correct when it sat first or last, wrong when it sat fourth to seventh. The model had the passage and did not use it.

Liu et al. tested exactly this. Same question, same documents, same total length; only the position of the document with the answer moved. Accuracy was highest at the beginning and end and dropped in the middle, and the drop deepened as the input grew.

This changes what "more context" means. Sending ten chunks "to be safe" pushes the good ones towards the middle and adds passages that are related but wrong, and those compete with the right one.

Placement is done by your code, so it is enforced. Whether the model then uses the passage is not; you can only raise the odds and check the result.

The trade: fewer chunks risks leaving the answer out; more chunks risks the model not using it. Only end-to-end accuracy tells you which you are paying.

How it works

The shape to remember. The values are illustrative; the shape is the finding.

Before fixing anything, find out which problem you have.

What the log shows Meaning Fix
right when the answer chunk is first or last, wrong when it is in the middle position: present and unused fewer chunks; best at the ends
equally wrong at every position the chunks are plausible and wrong the retriever or reranker
wrong mostly when the question shares no words with the passage an inference step is needed better retrieval; smaller input
wrong when similar passages are present distractors filter; fewer chunks
Rule What actually happens
Shrink first Going from ten chunks to four after a reranker loses a little recall and removes most of the middle. It also cuts cost and time to first token.
Then place Best chunk first, second-best last, weakest in the middle; the question at the very end. The reordering itself is owned by the RAG reordering note.
Placement trusts the ranker If the true answer is ranked seventh, edge placement has put it in the worst spot on purpose.
Past a point, split A question that needs forty documents has no small set to place. Extract per document in separate calls, then combine the extracts in one short call.

Conceptually, two pulls make the U: text near the end is closest to where generation starts, and training data teaches that openings matter. In practice the exact cause is still debated; the shape is what is well established, and the shape is what you design against.

Evolution

Lineage:Jul 2023 the U-curve measuredApr 2024 RULER: usable length below advertisedFeb 2025 NoLiMa: far worse when the answer needs inferenceJul 2025 decay and distractor effects measured on 18 current models2025–26 provider guides say "documents at the top, question at the end"
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026).
  • Stronger-model test: partly. Newer models show a shallower dip at a given length, and windows have grown, which makes a larger middle. What won't change: presence is not use, so recall alone cannot certify an answer.
  • Checked on: GPT-3.5-era and extended-context models (2023); 18 models in the 2025 study. Depth differs by model and length, so re-measure after a model change.

Code

The quote-first check: it improves grounding and gives code something to verify.

def answer(question, chunks, llm):
    docs = "\n".join(f"<doc id='{c.id}'>{c.text}</doc>" for c in chunks)      # already reranked and placed
    out = llm(f"{docs}\n<question>{question}</question>\n"                    # ① question last
              "First copy the exact sentence you rely on inside <quote> tags, then answer.")   # ② evidence first
    quote = extract(out, "quote")
    if not any(quote in c.text for c in chunks):                              # ③ the quote must exist in what was sent
        metrics.incr("answer.quote_not_found"); return retry_or_abstain(question)
    return out

Break it: the belief that a retrieved list is already in the best order.

ranked = ["r1", "r2", "r3", "r4", "r5"]                         # best first, as a reranker returns them
head, tail = ranked[0::2], ranked[1::2]                          # r1 r3 r5 | r2 r4
print(ranked, "→", head + tail[::-1])
# look for: r2 moved from second place to last place; r5 now in the middle
# naive belief predicts: the reranker's order is already the right prompt order

Run on Python 3.9, it prints ['r1', 'r2', 'r3', 'r4', 'r5'] → ['r1', 'r3', 'r5', 'r4', 'r2']. Rank order puts the second-best chunk next to the best; edge order puts it in the other strong position and the weakest in the dip.

Measure it

  • Offline: answer accuracy bucketed by the position of the answer-bearing chunk, against the same questions with that chunk moved. A gap between buckets is this effect; no gap means look at retrieval.
  • In production: the share of answers whose quoted evidence is not found in the chunks sent, and the gap between retrieval recall and answer accuracy over time.
  • Enforced by: assembly order and the chunk count, which are code. The quote check detects when the model did not use what it was given; nothing forces it to.

Interview

30-second answer: Models don't use a long context uniformly. Liu's 2023 study moved the answer-bearing document through a long input and found a U-shaped curve: accuracy high at the start and end, worse in the middle, including for long-context models. So the right chunk can be present and ignored. I mitigate by sending fewer, better chunks first, and by putting the best at the ends with the question last.

Q · Mechanism — Why would position matter if attention can reach every token? It can reach every token; nothing makes it reach them equally. Position schemes favour nearby tokens, which helps content close to the end, where generation begins. Training data favours openings: documents state their point first. The middle gets neither advantage. And in a long input each token competes with far more others, which is why the dip deepens with length. I'd be honest that the full causal account is still open; the shape is what's established.

Q · Trade-off — Recall at 10 is 95%, answer accuracy is 70%. Retriever or prompt? Neither yet. The simpler step is a measurement: log where the answer chunk lands and bucket accuracy by position. If it's right at the ends and wrong in the middle, it's presentation, and the best fix is fewer chunks, four after a reranker instead of ten, because that removes the middle and cuts cost. Edge placement is the fallback when the count can't shrink. If accuracy is flat and low, the retriever is returning plausible wrong chunks.

Q · Failure — Reranking and edge placement helped, then stopped helping on some questions. Three limits. Questions that need many documents have no small set to place. A weak reranker makes placement harmful, because the real answer gets ranked seventh and buried. And some failures aren't positional: related-but-wrong passages lower accuracy wherever they sit, and answers needing an inference step degrade faster than word-matching ones. I'd confirm by tagging failures by type. The fixes are filtering, better retrieval, or splitting into per-document calls.

Q · Design — Q&A over 500-page contracts, where the answer may be anywhere. No single call should see the whole document, so the system builds a small, precise context per question: chunk on clause boundaries, retrieve with keyword and vector search together, rerank to about five chunks, place by rank, question last, quote first. For "find every conflicting clause" questions, extract per section in parallel and combine the extracts. I'd watch accuracy by answer-chunk position first. The retrieval side is in the document QA design.

Compare

Mitigation What it does Cost Limit
Fewer chunks removes the middle some recall the answer may be left out
Edge placement best material at both ends a reranker only as good as the ranking
Question last, or at both ends the task sits next to generation a few tokens small effect on short inputs
Quote first evidence is surfaced and checkable output tokens detects, doesn't prevent
Split into per-document calls many short inputs N calls latency and cost
A bigger window nothing: a larger middle more tokens makes it worse

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Position effect highest at start and end, "significantly" lower in the middle multi-document QA and key-value retrieval; models of 2023, including extended-context ones cited (paper): Liu et al.
Question placement "up to 30 percent" better with the query at the end the vendor's own tests on complex multi-document inputs cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026): Anthropic guide

Pitfalls

  • "Long-context models have solved this"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: needle-in-a-haystack charts for new models are almost entirely green.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: those tests reward word matching. The 2023 study found the effect in long-context models, and later studies on current models still find decay with length.
    ↳ Think instead: a bigger window is a bigger middle.
  • "If retrieval recall is high, the answer will be right"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: recall is the metric the retrieval team already tracks.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: recall measures presence. Use depends on position, length and what else is in the window.
    ↳ Think instead: measure accuracy by where the answer chunk sat.
  • "Sending ten chunks is a safe hedge; extra ones are ignored"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: more evidence can't hurt a careful reader.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the extra chunks are not ignored, they compete. They push good chunks inward and add related-but-wrong text, which lowers accuracy.
    ↳ Think instead: each extra chunk is paid for in attention, not only in tokens.
  • Not the same: lost in the middle vs context rot
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "long inputs go wrong".
    ↳ Difference: this is about where a fixed piece of content sits. Context rot is decay from length and from stale or wrong content, wherever it sits.
    ↳ Think instead: reordering fixes the first only; see context rot.
  • Don't reorder things whose order carries meaning.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: edge placement worked on retrieved chunks.
    ↳ What goes wrong: conversation turns, logs, stack traces and numbered steps lose their sense when shuffled.
    ↳ Do instead: reorder only independent items; shorten or summarise sequences.
  • Don't build placement logic for three chunks.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it is a known best practice.
    ↳ What goes wrong: with three or four chunks there is no real middle, and the work buys nothing.
    ↳ Do instead: spend the effort on retrieval quality.
  • Shelf life: "present is not used" and "shrink first" are durable. The depth of the dip on a given model, and vendor placement advice, change.

Connections

  • Owned elsewhere: reordering and retrieve many, rerank few (RAG) cover the chunk-level mechanics; context utilization (LLM-Production) covers the benchmarks.
  • Used by delimiters and structure: why thirty tagged documents still fail.
  • Measured by component vs end-to-end eval: recall is the component, accuracy the result.
  • Drilled in instruction at the top or the bottom.

notes.title: Instruction Placement — Framing at the Top, the Task at the Bottom
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: prompting best practices · Liu et al. 2023: Lost in the Middle · Chroma 2025: Context Rot · Anthropic: prompt caching

TL;DR

In a short prompt, where an instruction sits barely matters. In a long one it does: an instruction above 20,000 tokens of documents has to survive all of them. The rule that satisfies both quality and caching: stable framing first, bulk data next, this request's task last. For the one rule you cannot afford to lose, state it at both ends.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchdesign time
Flow:system: role, standing rules, output contracttoolslong documents, delimitedthe question"quote first"the one critical rule againgeneration starts here

Recall

Prompt Answer
The rule for a long prompt? Long data near the top; the question and task instruction at the bottom.
Why doesn't it matter at 500 tokens? Nothing is far from anything.
The cheap hedge? Repeat the one critical constraint at the end.

The idea

A contract-analysis prompt begins "Answer only from the documents. Give the notice period in days." Then come thirty pages of contract. The answer comes back in months, with a clause from general knowledge mixed in. The same instruction moved below the documents gives the right answer.

Two things were working against the instruction at the top. Generation starts at the end of the input, and text near the end is used most reliably, so the instruction was as far from the action as it could be. And between it and the answer sat thirty pages full of their own imperative sentences ("the supplier must give notice…"), which the model had to tell apart from yours.

Two different kinds of text are being called "instructions". Framing (who you are, standing rules, output contract) is stable, belongs in the system message, and works from the top because the system role carries its own weight. The task for this request (the question, what to do with the documents) is small, changes every time, and wants to be the last thing read.

The trade: restating a rule at the end costs tens of tokens; two copies of a rule can drift apart, so repeat one rule, not ten.

How it works

The layout of a long prompt, top to bottom.

Region Changes every Cached Why it sits here
Tool definitions deploy yes large and stable; first in the cache order
System: role, standing rules, output contract deploy yes framing, not a task; the role marker carries it
Long documents, each in a tag with its source session or request if fixed for the session bulk goes above the question
The question and task instruction request no adjacent to generation
"Quote the sentence you rely on, then answer" request no shapes the first tokens written, so it is read last
The one critical rule, restated request no the sandwich: a hedge for both ends

In practice, Anthropic's guide (Oct 2026) says the same for its models: put long documents near the top, above the query, instructions and examples, and reports up to 30 percent better responses in its own tests with the query at the end.

Rule What actually happens
Distance is the problem, not the top A system prompt at the top works. A task instruction separated from the output by a long span of undifferentiated text is what fails.

Evolution

Lineage:2020–22 short prompts: placement is noiseJul 2023 position effects measured2023–24 provider guides: documents first, query last2024 prompt caching adds a second reason for stable-first
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026).
  • Stronger-model test: partly. Newer models hold a top-placed instruction over longer spans. What won't change: the question is the part that changes per request, so it belongs after everything that doesn't, for the cache if not for quality.

Code

Break it: the belief that restating a rule at the bottom spoils the cache.

import os
prefix = "SYSTEM RULES … " * 400 + "<doc>contract text … </doc>" * 200      # stable for the session
ask = lambda q: prefix + f"<question>{q}</question>\nAnswer only from the documents above."   # rule restated last
a, b = ask("notice period?"), ask("governing law?")
shared = len(os.path.commonprefix([a, b]))
print(shared == len(prefix) + len("<question>"), round(shared / len(a), 3))
# look for: True, and a shared share close to 1.0
# naive belief predicts: the restated rule breaks the shared prefix

Run on Python 3.9, it prints True 0.995. The restated rule sits below the last cache breakpoint and costs only its own few tokens.

Measure it

  • Offline: adherence to the task instruction (right unit, right source) with the instruction at the top, at the bottom and at both ends, on long inputs from the golden set. Keep the cheapest layout that holds.
  • In production: rate of answers that break the restated rule (a quote not found in the documents, a wrong unit), per prompt version.
  • Enforced by: the template, which fixes the order. That the model follows the last-placed instruction is a request only; the quote check in lost in the middle is what detects a miss.

Interview

30-second answer: At short lengths placement is noise. At long ones, an instruction buried above tens of thousands of tokens of documents competes with everything after it. So: stable framing first in the system message, bulk data next, and this request's question and task instruction last, right before generation. I restate the one rule I can't lose at the end. That layout also keeps the cacheable prefix intact.

Q · Mechanism — Why would the same instruction work at the bottom and not at the top? Two effects stack. Position: generation begins at the end, and text near the end is used most reliably, so an adjacent instruction has an advantage over one twenty thousand tokens back. Interference: between a top instruction and the output sit the documents, full of imperative language of their own, and distance makes separating yours from theirs harder.

Q · Trade-off — The cache wants the stable prompt first; position wants instructions last. Which wins? The simpler view is that they rarely conflict, because they're about different text. The system prompt is stable framing and goes first for both reasons. The per-request task is small and changing and goes last for both reasons.

Pitfalls

  • "Instructions go in the system prompt, so placement is handled"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the system prompt is where instructions live.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it holds framing. The task for this request is a different piece of text, and putting it above the documents is a placement choice even if nobody made it on purpose.
    ↳ Think instead: framing at the top, the task at the bottom.
  • "Repeating the instruction at the end is padding; the model already read it"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: duplication looks untidy, and I left it out for that reason.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: reading a rule and weighting it when generation starts are different things. The repeat costs tens of tokens on a prompt of thousands.
    ↳ Think instead: restate the one rule whose violation you can't accept.
  • Not the same: the system prompt vs the task instruction
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "instructions" written by you.
    ↳ Difference: one is identical on every request and describes the job in general; the other names what to do with this input and changes each time.
    ↳ Think instead: sort text by how often it changes; that decides where it sits.
  • Don't move the system prompt to the bottom.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "instructions last" sounds like it should apply to all of them.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you lose the cacheable prefix and gain almost nothing, since the role marker already gives that text its weight.
    ↳ Do instead: leave the system prompt first and move only the per-request task.
  • Shelf life: "stable first, task last" is durable, being backed by both caching and position. How far an instruction can sit from the output before it weakens is model-specific.

Connections

  • Builds on system, user and prefill: which message carries which text.
  • Costed in ordering for the cache: why the same layout is also the cheap one.
  • Drilled in instruction at the top or the bottom.

notes.title: Context Ordering for Prompt-Cache Hit Rate — Stable First, One Byte Can Cost the Prefix
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: prompt caching · OpenAI: prompt caching · Gemini API: context caching · Anthropic: context editing · Anthropic Engineering: effective context engineering for AI agents

TL;DR

A prompt cache matches from the first token up to the first difference. Everything after that point is paid in full. So order is the whole lever: what never changes goes first, what always changes goes last, and nothing that changes may sit in the stable part. One timestamp near the top makes every request a miss, and nothing reports it as an error.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:tools (sorted, canonical)shared system textper-config system promptsession documenthistory, append-onlyretrieved textdate + questioncache read

Recall

Prompt Answer
The one rule? Stable prefix first, changing content last.
Cost of one early change? Everything after it misses the cache.
Anthropic's prefix order? tools → system → messages; a change at one level invalidates the rest.
The metric, and its grain? Cache-read tokens over input tokens, per route and per config.
What fights the cache? Eviction: trimming history rewrites the prefix.
Draw by hand: the zones Global text, config text, session document, then history, retrieved text, question; a breakpoint after each of the first three.

The idea

A team turns on prompt caching and the bill does not move. The usage data shows cache writes on every request and no reads. The system prompt begins: "Current time: 2026-10-11 14:03:22."

The cache holds the model's computed state for a run of tokens, and that state depends on every token before it. Identical text is reusable only up to the first token that differs. A timestamp on line one differs on every request, so the reusable run has length zero, and each request pays the write premium to store something that will never be read.

Move the timestamp to the end, next to the question, and nothing else changes: the model still knows the time, and several thousand tokens of system prompt and tool definitions are now read from the cache.

The hit is therefore a length: how many leading tokens matched. The design goal is to make that run as long as possible, which is purely a question of what you put where.

Because this is assembly code, the order is enforced on every request. What you must guard against is your own code leaking something changeable into the stable part.

The trade: a cache-friendly order costs nothing at run time. It constrains the design: what you allow to vary per request, and how often you may rewrite history.

How it works

Sort every piece of the prompt by how often it changes, slowest first.

Region Changes every Cached Note
Tool definitions deploy yes serialise with sorted keys and a fixed tool order
Platform-wide system text deploy yes the most shared span of all
— breakpoint 1 —
Per-config system prompt, fixed examples config version yes no dates, no user names, no request ids
— breakpoint 2 —
Session document or workspace session yes fixed for the session, so it belongs up here
— breakpoint 3 —
Conversation history turn yes, while append-only each turn extends a valid prefix
Retrieved text request no placed after everything stable
Date, user details, the question request no last

Three zones and three breakpoints are enough; Anthropic allows up to four per request (Oct 2026).

What breaks the prefix How it shows up Fix
A date or time in the system prompt hit rate drops to zero at midnight, or always move it to the end
Tool or feature lists rendered in unstable order hit rate changes with the number of server processes sort; canonical JSON
A per-user string above the breakpoint writes with no reads move it below
A tool toggled per request everything misses when it flips keep the tool set fixed per config
Trimming history a little each turn tokens fall and cost rises evict rarely, in one large step
Stable and changing text interleaved only the first stable block is ever read group all stable text first

Why only a prefix can match, the prices and the lifetimes are in provider prompt caching.

Evolution

Lineage:2023 order chosen for quality only2024 provider prompt caching makes order a cost decision2024–25 automatic caching: on by default, still prefix-only2025 server-side context clearing, with a minimum-cleared setting to justify the cache rewrite
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026).
  • Stronger-model test: no. This is a property of how a transformer computes, not a weakness of a model generation. What won't change: cached state for a token depends on everything before it, so only a prefix can be reused.
  • Checked on: the prefix order and breakpoint limit are Anthropic's as of Oct 2026; OpenAI and Google give the same advice (stable content first) for their automatic caches.

Code

Assembly with the zones made explicit.

def canonical_tools(tools):                                        # tools sit above everything: an unstable
    return json.dumps(sorted(tools, key=lambda t: t["name"]),      # order here costs the whole prefix
                      sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))

def build(cfg, session, turn):
    return [
        text(PLATFORM_INSTRUCTIONS, cache=True),            # zone 1: identical for every tenant
        text(cfg.system_prompt, cache=True),                # zone 2: fixed per config version; never a date here
        text(session.pinned_doc, cache=True),               # zone 3: fixed for the session
        *session.history,                                   # append-only: the prefix keeps growing
        text(render(turn.retrieved)),                       # changes per request: below every breakpoint
        text(f"Today is {turn.date}\n{turn.question}"),     # the date lives here
    ]

Break it: the belief that the same tools produce the same prompt.

import json, os
tools = [{"name": "search", "args": {"q": "str", "k": "int"}}, {"name": "lookup", "args": {"id": "str"}}]
filler = "SYSTEM PROMPT … " * 300
a = json.dumps(tools) + filler
b = json.dumps(tools[::-1]) + filler                           # another process lists the tools in another order
canon = lambda t: json.dumps(sorted(t, key=lambda x: x["name"]), sort_keys=True)
print(len(os.path.commonprefix([a, b])), "of", len(a), "|", canon(tools) == canon(tools[::-1]))
# look for: a shared prefix of a few characters out of thousands, then True
# naive belief predicts: the full length, because the content is the same

Run on Python 3.9, it prints 11 of 4897 | True. Two servers that list the same tools in a different order share eleven characters of prefix; sorted, they share all of it.

Measure it

  • Offline: render the prefix twice for the same config, in two processes, and compare bytes; any difference is a bug. Then replay a session and total the cache-read share against the unordered layout.
  • In production: cache-read tokens over total input tokens, per config version and per tenant, against each one's own trailing baseline; read it beside the eviction count, since the two interact.
  • Enforced by: the assembler, plus a deploy check that rejects any fragment whose rendering is not byte-identical across two runs.

Interview

30-second answer: Prompt caches are prefix caches: the provider reuses computed state for the longest unchanged run from the start of the request, so the first differing token invalidates everything after it. I put stable things first, tool schemas, system prompt, fixed examples, session document, and changing things last: retrieved chunks, the date, the question. The subtlety is that eviction fights this, because dropping old content rewrites the prefix.

Q · Mechanism — Why can't the cache match content wherever it sits? Because what is stored is the attention state for each token, and that state depends on every token before it. Change token 50 and the stored state for token 51 onward describes a sequence that no longer exists. So a hit is a length, not a yes or no: if the first 8,000 tokens match and token 8,001 differs, 8,000 are read at the cached price and the rest are paid in full. Maximising that length is an ordering problem.

Q · Trade-off — Long-context advice says documents at the top; caching says changing content at the bottom. The simpler question dissolves most of it: how often does the document change? In a chat-with-this-PDF product it is fixed for the session, so it goes in the stable prefix: early for quality and cached across turns. Per-request retrieved chunks can't be cached wherever they sit, so position alone decides, and they go after the stable part. The real conflict is a large document that changes every request; there I measure the accuracy change and price the miss.

Q · Failure — Hit rate fell from 80% to 20% overnight with no deploy. In order: something non-deterministic in the prefix, like tool schemas serialised in unstable order, which shows up after a scale-out. A date in the system prompt, which shows up at midnight. Routing: more concurrency spreading identical prefixes across machines. And traffic: cache lifetimes are minutes, so a quieter route stops staying warm. I'd confirm from the hour the drop began and from write and read counts per config.

Q · Design — Prompt assembly for 200 agent configs across many tenants, tuned for hit rate. One careless byte destroys cacheability, and 200 configs will contain it. So the assembler owns the prefix: tenants supply versioned fragments, the platform renders them canonically, and a deploy check rejects any fragment that renders differently twice. Three zones, platform, config, session, each with a breakpoint, and anything per-request is forced below. I'd watch hit rate per config against its own baseline. The surrounding layers are in the prompt-layer reference architecture.

Pitfalls

  • "Caching is automatic, so there is nothing to design"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: several providers now cache without being asked.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: automatic means you don't switch it on. It still matches only a prefix, so a timestamp at the top gives a hit rate near zero and no error.
    ↳ Think instead: the provider supplies the cache; you supply the prefix.
  • "Cache hit rate is one number for the service"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: dashboards start with an average.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it is per prefix, so per route, config and tenant. A healthy average hides one config near zero, and that config is paying full price.
    ↳ Think instead: track it per config against its own history.
  • "Putting today's date in the system prompt is harmless"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the model needs the date, and the system prompt is where context goes.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: sitting above everything, it invalidates the whole prefix daily, or on every request with a time. I looked for that cost regression in retrieval volume, where it wasn't.
    ↳ Think instead: anything that changes goes below everything that doesn't.
  • Not the same: ordering for the cache vs ordering for attention
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both produce a rule about what goes first.
    ↳ Difference: the cache sorts by how often text changes. Attention sorts by how important text is to this answer. They usually agree; they differ for large per-request documents.
    ↳ Think instead: sort by change rate first, then place within the changing part for quality.
  • Don't freeze something that should vary just to cache it.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a fixed example block or a pinned document makes the hit-rate chart look better.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you trade accuracy for cost without having measured either.
    ↳ Do instead: measure the accuracy change, price the miss, then decide.
  • Don't pair caching with a little eviction every turn.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: both are cost optimisations, so together they should save more.
    ↳ What goes wrong: each trim rewrites the prefix, so tokens go down while cost goes up.
    ↳ Do instead: evict rarely and in bulk; see conversation history.

notes.title: Provider Prompt Caching — Paying Once for a Prefix You Send Every Time
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: prompt caching · OpenAI: prompt caching · Gemini API: context caching · vLLM: automatic prefix caching · Anthropic Engineering: effective context engineering for AI agents

TL;DR

The provider keeps the model's computed state for the start of your prompt and reuses it when the next request starts the same way. You pay about a tenth for those tokens and skip the time to process them. It caches your input, not the answer: the output is generated fresh every time. Two catches: the first request pays more than normal to write the entry, and entries expire in minutes.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:request 1prefix processed in fullentry stored (5 min)
request 2, same prefix, inside the lifetimeonly the new suffix is processedfresh outputthe lifetime restarts

Recall

Prompt Answer
What is stored? The model's internal state for a prefix of tokens; not the text, not the response.
Why only a prefix? Each token's state depends on every token before it.
The two prices? Reads about 0.1× input; writes above 1× (1.25× or 2× on Anthropic).
Does it change the output? No. The same tokens reach the model.
How do you know it worked? The usage fields: cache-read and cache-write tokens per response.
Draw by hand: two calls Call 1: app → provider, full processing, entry written. Call 2: prefix read from cache, only the suffix processed.

The idea

A document-chat product sends a 50,000-token contract with every question. A user asks twenty questions; the product pays to process the same 50,000 tokens twenty times, and each answer waits for all of them to be read again.

Nothing about the contract changed between question one and question two. The work the model did to read it, an internal state for each token, could have been kept. Prompt caching keeps it. Question two arrives, the provider sees the same leading tokens, loads the stored state, and processes only the new question. The 50,000 tokens are billed at a small fraction and the first token arrives sooner.

The model still writes a new answer each time. Nothing about the response is stored, so an answer cannot be stale, and two identical requests can still give different outputs.

The first request is the catch. Writing the entry costs more than an ordinary request, so caching is a bet that the prefix will be used again before it expires.

The trade: a large saving in cost and latency on a repeated prefix, for a write premium on first use and a design that must keep that prefix byte-identical.

How it works

Two requests in the same session.

The entry lives on the provider's machines, so a hit also depends on your request reaching a machine that holds it.

Whether caching pays is one inequality.

cost without cache = N · P · r                       ← N requests, P prefix tokens, r price per input token
cost with cache    = P · r · w + (N − 1) · P · r · h ← one write at multiplier w, then reads at multiplier h
caching wins when    N > (w − h) / (1 − h)           ← w = 1.25, h = 0.1 → N > 1.28: the second request pays
                                                     ← w = 2 (1-hour entry) → N > 2.1: the third request pays
Rule What actually happens
The first call always pays A route where each prefix is used once pays the write premium for nothing.
Lifetime makes it a traffic question A prefix used a hundred times a minute stays warm; one used twice an hour never hits. Prompt design can't fix a low request rate.
A minimum length applies Below the provider's minimum nothing is cached and no error is raised.
Cached tokens still fill the window Caching changes the price of those tokens, not whether they count towards the limit.
Parallel first requests all miss On Anthropic an entry is usable only after the first response begins, so send one request, then fan out.

How to arrange the prompt so the prefix stays identical is context ordering. How a server keeps and reuses this state internally is owned by the LLM-Production pillar's notes on efficient serving.

Evolution

Lineage:within one request, state reused token to token (always)mid-2024 Google context caching; Aug 2024 Anthropic explicit breakpointsOct 2024 OpenAI automatic caching2025 one-hour and 24-hour lifetimes; implicit caching on Gemini2026 automatic and explicit modes offered side by side
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): the mechanism is settled; prices, lifetimes, minimums and modes changed at every provider in the past year.
  • Stronger-model test: no. It is a property of serving, and newer models made it cheaper: read multipliers on the newest models are below 0.1×. What won't change: only an identical prefix can be reused, and the first use costs more than the rest.
  • Checked on: every multiplier, lifetime and minimum in this note was read from the provider pages on 11 Oct 2026.

Code

Explicit breakpoints on Anthropic's API, and the measurement that says whether they worked.

MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # as of Oct 2026
resp = client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024, tools=TOOLS,                 # tools come first in the prefix order
    system=[{"type": "text", "text": SYSTEM_PROMPT,
             "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}],         # breakpoint 1: 5-minute entry
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "text", "text": session.document,
         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}}, # breakpoint 2: 2× to write, worth it per session
        {"type": "text", "text": f"{today}\n{question}"},      # changing text last, never in system
    ]}],
)
u = resp.usage                                                 # the only ground truth
total_in = u.input_tokens + u.cache_read_input_tokens + u.cache_creation_input_tokens
metrics.gauge("cache.read_share", u.cache_read_input_tokens / max(total_in, 1), tags={"cfg": cfg.version})
metrics.gauge("cache.write_tokens", u.cache_creation_input_tokens, tags={"cfg": cfg.version})

Break it: the belief that turning caching on always saves money.

def cost(n, prefix=50_000, w=1.25, h=0.1):            # in units of "one input token at base price"
    return prefix * n, prefix * w + prefix * h * (n - 1)
for n in (1, 2, 20):
    plain, cached = cost(n)
    print(n, int(plain), int(cached))
# look for: at n = 1 the cached column is the larger one
# naive belief predicts: cached is never more expensive

Run on Python 3.9, it prints 1 50000 62500, 2 100000 67500 and 20 1000000 157500. One use costs a quarter more than not caching; twenty uses cost under a sixth.

Measure it

  • Offline: replay recorded sessions through the cost formula with and without caching, per route, using each route's real gaps between requests against the lifetime.
  • In production: cache-read share and cache-write tokens per config. Writes with no reads mean a prefix that is never reused or never identical; a read share that follows the time of day means traffic or routing.
  • Enforced by: the provider, for matching and expiry. Your code enforces only that the prefix is identical; the usage fields are how you find out it wasn't.

Interview

30-second answer: When a model processes a prompt it computes internal state for every token, which is most of the cost of a long input. Prompt caching keeps that state for a prefix and reuses it when the next request starts with the same tokens, so I pay about a tenth for the cached part and skip its processing time. The catches: writes cost more than normal, and entries expire in minutes.

Q · Mechanism — What exactly is stored, and why can't it match anywhere in the prompt? The key and value tensors the attention layers computed for a span of tokens: the structure the model builds anyway while reading, kept instead of discarded. Not the text and not the response. It only matches from the start because the state for token n depends on every earlier token; change anything before it and the stored state describes a sequence that no longer exists. It's the within-request cache made to survive across requests.

Q · Trade-off — Explicit breakpoints or automatic caching? The simpler rung is automatic: nothing to configure, and a team that never thought about caching gets some benefit. Explicit breakpoints buy control over where the boundaries sit when the prompt has several stability zones, and a choice of longer lifetime for the spans that justify it. The cost is responsibility: a breakpoint above something that changes means paying write premiums forever, silently. I'd write the assembler to be prefix-stable either way, since that works under both.

Q · Failure — At peak traffic the hit rate falls although prompts are identical. The cache isn't one global service. An entry sits with the machines that computed it, so as concurrency rises identical prefixes land where they've never been seen. I'd confirm by plotting read share against concurrency and time of day. Fixes: a stable cache key where the provider offers one, fewer and more widely shared prefixes, and warming with one request before fanning out. Low-traffic tenants show the opposite problem: entries expire between their requests.

Q · Design — You move from a hosted API to serving the model yourself. What happens to the caching strategy? The mechanism survives; the economics change. Self-hosted prefix caching reuses the same state, and there is no per-token price, so the gain becomes throughput and time to first token. I gain control of how long entries stay and of routing same-prefix requests to the same replica. The new tension is memory: cached state competes with the room for concurrent requests. So I'd watch tokens per second per GPU first, with hit rate underneath. The platform side is self-hosted vs API.

Compare

Anthropic OpenAI Gemini API Self-hosted (vLLM)
Mode explicit breakpoints, or automatic placement automatic; explicit on newer models implicit; explicit cache objects automatic, block level
You control where boundaries sit; 5-minute or 1-hour entries a routing key; retention setting cache objects memory, eviction, routing
You pay a write premium, a low read price a low read price; a write premium on newer models savings passed on GPU memory, not money
Main risk a breakpoint above changing text assuming automatic means long prefix entries you can't see cache crowding out concurrency

Dated multipliers, lifetimes and minimums for the three hosted providers are in the chapter map's Landscape table.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Read multiplier 0.1× base input; lower on the newest models Anthropic; OpenAI GPT-5.6 and later cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026): provider docs
Write multiplier 1.25× (5-minute), 2× (1-hour) Anthropic; 1.25× on OpenAI GPT-5.6 and later cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026)
Break-even second request (w = 1.25); third (w = 2) N > (w − h) / (1 − h) with h = 0.1 derived

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: a prompt cache vs a response cache
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "caching for LLM calls" and both cut cost.
    ↳ Difference: a prompt cache reuses work on your input and still generates a fresh answer. A response cache returns a stored answer and can be stale or wrong for a slightly different question.
    ↳ Think instead: one is a billing and latency feature with no effect on output; the other is a product decision with a correctness risk (caching strategy).
  • "Enabling caching always saves money"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the headline is a 90% discount.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a write costs more than an uncached request. A route that writes and never reads pays a premium on every call, and nothing errors.
    ↳ Think instead: caching is a bet on reuse within the lifetime; check the usage fields.
  • "The cache is a service: if the prefix matches, it hits"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: that is how a key-value store behaves.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a hit needs the request to reach a machine holding the entry, before it expires. I took a peak-hour dip for a bug in prompt assembly; it was routing.
    ↳ Think instead: hit rate depends on prefix, traffic rate and routing together.
  • "Cached tokens are free room in the window"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: they are nearly free on the bill.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: they still occupy the context window and still compete for the model's attention.
    ↳ Think instead: caching changes the price of a token, not its presence.
  • Don't use the discount to justify a bloated prompt.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: at a tenth of the price, extra context looks harmless.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a tenth of the price for tokens the model didn't need is still a cost, and over-full windows answer worse.
    ↳ Do instead: trim first, then cache what remains.
  • Shelf life: "a prefix, written once, read cheaply, expiring" is durable. Every number here is not: re-read the provider page before quoting one.

Connections

Path:window budgetingprovider prompt cachingordering for the cachecaching strategy
  • Builds on what prompting is: the prefix is reusable computation.
  • Used by ordering for the cache: keeping the prefix identical.
  • Breaks when combined with history rewriting on every turn: each rewrite is a new write.
  • Owned elsewhere: latency metrics (LLM-Production) covers time to first token, which a cache read shortens.
  • Costed in cost modelling: the cached share of a monthly bill.
  • Drilled in prompt caching and ordering.

notes.title: Context Compression — Five Ways to Shrink the Window, and What Each One Loses
notes.html:
References

Jiang et al. 2023: LLMLingua · Jiang et al. 2023: LongLLMLingua · Pan et al. 2024: LLMLingua-2 · Anthropic: context editing

TL;DR

Compression trades fidelity for tokens. Five ways, from safest to riskiest: drop it, move it out and keep a handle, extract exact spans, prune tokens, summarise with a model. Dropping loses content and you know it. Summarising can lose or invent content without anyone knowing, and the error is then read by every later turn. Compression is itself a step with latency, cost and a failure mode. Try dropping first.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:over budgetspent content? drop itlarge payload? store it, keep a handlemust quote it? extract spanslong plain prose? prune tokensaccumulated decisions? structured summarycheck the pinned facts survived

Recall

Prompt Answer
The five options? Drop, externalise to a handle, extract spans, prune tokens, summarise.
Which loss is the dangerous kind? Summarising: omission or invention that nothing flags.
What should a summary look like? A schema (decisions, constraints, open questions), not free prose.

The idea

A long planning session is compressed every few turns with "summarise the conversation so far". On turn three the user said "no breaking changes to the public API". On turn thirty the agent proposes renaming a public endpoint, confidently. The constraint was in the transcript. It was not in the summary, and nothing in the system noticed it had gone.

Had the old turns simply been dropped, the loss would at least have been known. The summary gave the appearance of memory while quietly leaving out the one thing that mattered, and every later turn then reasoned from the summary as if it were complete.

So order the options by how visible their loss is. Raw tool results the model has already used can just go. A large payload can move to storage, leaving a reference the agent can re-read. Evidence you must quote should be cut down to exact sentences. A model-written summary comes last, and when you need one, give it a shape: fields for decisions, constraints, identifiers and open questions. A missing field is visible; a missing sentence in a paragraph is not.

The trade: every option saves tokens; they differ in whether the loss is known, and in what the compression step itself costs.

How it works

A summary is gated: it replaces the original only if the facts you pinned are still in it.

The purple step is the only one that can invent or omit; the check after it is ordinary code.

Rule What actually happens
Pruning keeps the surprising tokens A small model scores each token by how predictable it is; predictable ones are dropped. The result reads as damaged English and stays usable to the large model.
Pruning corrupts exact content A dropped token in a number, an identifier, code or a legal clause is a wrong value, not a rougher sentence. Prose only.
Never summarise a summary without an anchor Repeated summarising drifts. The goal and hard constraints stay verbatim, outside the summary, for the whole session.

Compressing retrieved chunks specifically is owned by the RAG note on context compression and filtering.

Evolution

Lineage:2023 "summarise the history" as a framework defaultOct 2023 LLMLingua: pruning by token predictabilityMar 2024 LLMLingua-2: a trained, task-agnostic compressorSep 2025 server-side clearing of old tool results2025–26 server-side compaction in beta
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): dropping and summarising are routine; token pruning stays a niche; provider-side compaction is still beta at the provider read for this note.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. Larger windows postpone the need, and stronger models write better summaries. What won't change: compression is lossy by construction, so the question is always whether the facts the task depends on survived.

Code

The schema the summary must fill, and the check that gates it.

SUMMARY_FIELDS = ("decisions", "constraints", "identifiers", "open_questions")

def compact(old_turns, pinned_facts, llm):
    summary = llm.json(f"Fill these fields from the conversation: {SUMMARY_FIELDS}\n{render(old_turns)}")
    text = json.dumps(summary).lower()
    missing = [f for f in pinned_facts if f.lower() not in text]      # e.g. "no breaking changes"
    if missing:
        metrics.incr("compact.pinned_fact_lost", len(missing))        # the failure that used to be silent
        return old_turns                                              # keep the original this time
    return [as_message(summary)]

A substring check is crude and catches the worst case: a constraint that vanished.

Compare

Option How Loss Best for
Drop / clear remove it total, and known old raw tool results
Externalise store it, keep a reference none; a round trip to read it again large payloads and files
Extract spans keep exact sentences surrounding context evidence you must cite
Prune tokens drop predictable tokens with a small model readability; exactness long redundant prose
Summarise a model restates it omission and invention, hidden history with accumulated decisions

Measure it

  • Offline: task success on long-session fixtures with and without compression, and the share of pinned facts present after compaction. Readability of the summary is not a metric.
  • In production: pinned-fact losses, compactions per session, and the latency of the compaction call.
  • Enforced by: the code that chooses the option and the pinned-fact check. The summary's content is a request only.

Interview

30-second answer: Compression trades fidelity for tokens. The options run from dropping content, through moving it out behind a handle and extracting exact spans, to pruning tokens with a small model and summarising with a large one. Extraction and dropping are safest because the loss is known. Summarising is strongest and can silently omit a constraint, so I summarise into a schema and check that pinned facts survive.

Q · Mechanism — How does token pruning work without destroying the text? Language is redundant from a model's point of view: many tokens are predictable from context and carry little information. A small, cheap model scores each token by how surprising it is, and the least surprising are dropped under a budget per segment. The output isn't meant for a human reader.

Q · Trade-off — Summarise old turns, or drop them? The simpler rung is dropping, and it is right more often than people expect: free, instant, and the loss is known. A summary costs a model call and can omit the constraint from turn three with no signal. So I ask whether old turns hold state the task still needs. Self-contained support questions: drop, keep the last few. A long session where decisions pile up: a structured summary, recent turns verbatim, the original goal untouched.

Pitfalls

  • "Compression is lossless if the summary is good"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a well-written summary reads as complete.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it is lossy by design. The only question is whether the facts the task depends on survived, and reading the summary doesn't tell you.
    ↳ Think instead: validate against the task's pinned facts, not against how the summary reads.
  • "Compression is a cost optimisation"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it is usually introduced when the bill grows.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: removing stale and irrelevant content improves answers by itself. Framed as cost only, I squeezed the cheap, important parts and left the expensive, useless ones.
    ↳ Think instead: it is a quality step that also saves money; choose what to remove by relevance.
  • Not the same: compaction vs clearing
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are provider features that shrink a long conversation.
    ↳ Difference: clearing removes old tool results and leaves a placeholder; nothing is rewritten by a model. Compaction replaces history with a model-written summary.
    ↳ Think instead: clearing has a known loss; compaction has a hidden one and needs a check.
  • Don't compress what you can drop.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a summary feels safer than deletion.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you pay a model call to keep a rougher copy of something already used up.
    ↳ Do instead: clear spent tool results; reserve summarising for content that still carries state.
  • Shelf life: the ordering by visibility of loss is durable. Which of these the provider does for you is moving quickly.

Connections

Path:window budgetingcontext compressionconversation historycontext rot
  • Used by conversation history: the compressed middle tier.
  • Breaks when combined with cache ordering if run every turn: each rewrite is a cache miss.
  • Owned elsewhere: context compression and filtering (RAG) covers retrieved chunks.
