notes.title: Conversation History Management — Pin the Goal, Keep the Recent, Compact Rarely
notes.html:
References

LangChain: short-term memory · Anthropic: context editing · Anthropic: context windows · Chroma 2025: Context Rot

TL;DR

History is the part of the window that grows every turn, so every multi-turn system needs a rule for it. The rule that works has tiers: the user's goal pinned and never dropped, the last few turns verbatim, the middle compressed, long-lived facts stored outside. From the cache's point of view history is append-only: rewriting it costs a full cache write, so compact rarely and deeply.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:append each turntokens past the trigger?clear old raw tool resultsdonesummarise the middle into a schemakeep goal + last turns verbatimcontinue appending

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why not drop the oldest turns? The oldest turn is usually the user's goal.
What does rewriting history cost? The cached prefix: the next call pays a full write.
The tiers? Pinned goal, recent turns verbatim, compressed middle, memory outside the window.

The idea

A coding assistant keeps the last twenty messages and drops the rest. Around message twenty-five it starts refactoring a file the user never mentioned. The user's first message, "fix the failing login test, touch nothing else", slid out of the window five messages ago.

A sliding window treats history as a queue. History is not uniform. The first message carries the goal. The last few carry the task in progress and the most recent correction. The middle is mostly resolved detours and raw tool output that has already been used.

So give each part its own treatment. Pin the goal and any stated constraints: they are small and never leave. Keep the last three to five turns word for word. Replace the middle with a structured summary when space demands it. Facts that must outlive the session go to a store outside the window.

Then decide how often to act. A prompt cache reads the conversation as a growing prefix: each new turn extends what the previous call already stored. The moment you rewrite earlier turns, the prefix changes and the next call pays full price. A policy that trims a little every turn makes the token count go down and the bill go up.

The trade: keeping everything is cheapest per turn while it fits, and degrades quality as it grows; compacting restores quality and costs a cache rewrite each time.

How it works

The history region of the window, in tiers.

Region Changes every Cached Rule
Pinned: the user's goal and stated constraints session yes never dropped, never summarised
Structured summary of the middle compaction after it settles decisions, constraints, identifiers, open questions
Recent turns, verbatim (last 3–5) turn as appended never paraphrased
Current turn request no —
Rule What actually happens
Trigger on tokens, not turns Turns range from ten tokens to fifty thousand.
Tool results first Old raw tool results are the largest and least valuable part; clearing them needs no model call.
A minimum makes it worth it If an action would free too little to repay the cache rewrite, skip it this turn. Anthropic's clearing exposes this as clear_at_least.

How to compress the middle safely is context compression.

Evolution

Lineage:2022–23 buffer, sliding window and summary memory in frameworks2024 prompt caching makes append-only history the cheap patternSep 2025 server-side clearing of old tool results2025–26 server-side compaction
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): the tiered design is settled; provider features that do it for you are still beta.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. Larger windows and server-side compaction remove most hand-built trimming. What won't change: the goal must survive, recent turns must stay exact, and rewriting history costs the cache.
  • Checked on: Anthropic's context editing (beta, Oct 2026): clearing starts at 100,000 input tokens by default and keeps the three most recent tool uses.

Code

Break it: the belief that trimming a little every turn is the frugal policy.

def session_cost(turns=30, per_turn=2_000, trim_every_turn=False, w=1.25, h=0.1):
    cost, cached = 0.0, 0
    for t in range(1, turns + 1):
        size = min(t, 10) * per_turn if trim_every_turn else t * per_turn    # trimming caps the window at 10 turns
        reusable = 0 if trim_every_turn else cached                          # a rewritten prefix reuses nothing
        cost += reusable * h + (size - reusable) * w                         # read the old part, write the new
        cached = size
    return round(cost)
print(session_cost(), session_cost(trim_every_turn=True))
# look for: the trimmed session costs more although it sends fewer tokens
# naive belief predicts: fewer tokens, lower cost

Run on Python 3.9, it prints 162000 and 637500, in units of one input token at base price. Append-only pays mostly the read price; per-turn trimming pays the write price on everything, every turn.

Measure it

  • Offline: task success at turn 10, 20 and 40 on recorded long sessions, per strategy, with token-units per session.
  • In production: compactions per session, tokens freed per compaction, cache-read share before and after, and quality by turn depth.
  • Enforced by: the history policy in the assembler (pin, tiers, trigger, minimum). The summary's content is a request only and is checked as in context compression.

Interview

30-second answer: History grows every turn, so it needs a policy. I use tiers: pin the user's original goal so it's never evicted, keep the last few turns verbatim because the active task lives there, compress the middle into a structured summary, and put long-lived facts in a store outside the window. And since rewriting history invalidates the prompt cache, I compact rarely and deeply, triggered by tokens.

Q · Mechanism — Walk me through a history policy you'd ship. A pin plus three tiers. The pin is the goal and hard constraints: small, never evicted. Tier one is the last three to five turns, verbatim, because the task in progress and the latest correction live there. Tier two is the middle as a structured summary. The trigger is a token threshold, and compaction goes well below it so it doesn't fire again next turn.

Q · Trade-off — A rolling summary, or keep everything until the wall? The simpler rung is keeping everything, and it is better than it sounds because an append-only history is read from the cache at a fraction of the price. A rolling summary rewrites the prefix; run every turn, it raises cost while lowering tokens. The counter-pressure is quality, which slides with length before the wall. So: append while quality holds, then compact in one large step, with the trigger set from the eval and a minimum amount freed.

Pitfalls

  • "History management is only about fitting in the window"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: overflow is the failure that produces an error.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a conversation that fits can still answer worse, because twenty turns of finished detours compete with the current question.
    ↳ Think instead: manage history for relevance; size is the lesser reason.
  • "A sliding window is a sensible default; frameworks do it"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it is one parameter and it never overflows.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it drops the first message, where the user said what they wanted. The agents I saw "forget the goal" were running an unpinned window.
    ↳ Think instead: pin turn one, then slide over the middle.
  • Not the same: conversation history vs long-term memory
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "what the assistant remembers".
    ↳ Difference: history is in the window, costs tokens every turn and ends with the session. Memory is stored outside, fetched when needed, and can be wrong when fetched.
    ↳ Think instead: the window holds this conversation; a store holds what outlives it (long-term memory).
  • Don't summarise the recent turns.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: they are tokens like any others.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the active task lives there; a paraphrase loses the exact wording, numbers and corrections the model needs next.
    ↳ Do instead: compress the middle and leave both ends exact.
  • Shelf life: pin, tiers and "rarely and deeply" are durable. Trigger defaults and what the provider automates are volatile.

Connections

Path:window budgetingconversation historycontext compressionmulti-turn prompt design
  • Builds on ordering for the cache: why history is append-only.
  • Owned elsewhere: conversation memory and long-term memory (Agentic) cover memory across an agent's run and across sessions.
  • Used by context rot: what accumulates when no policy runs.
  • Drilled in drift by turn 30 and step 40: what to throw away.

notes.title: Context Rot & Context Pollution — When What Is Already in the Window Works Against You
notes.html:
References

Chroma 2025: Context Rot · Liu et al. 2023: Lost in the Middle · Modarressi et al. 2025: NoLiMa · Anthropic: context windows

TL;DR

Two related failures. Rot: answers get worse as the input grows, well before the window is full. Pollution: specific content, a failed tool call, a stale passage, the model's own earlier mistake, sits in the window and is treated as fact. Neither raises an error. The system keeps answering, slightly worse, on the long sessions nobody evaluates. The fix is per type of content, and sometimes the right fix is to start again with a clean window.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:turn N answerjoins the historyturn N+1 reads it as factslightly worse answerjoins the history…
break the loop: replace failures with a one-line notedrop stale passagesclear raw payloadsor restart from goal + constraints

Recall

Prompt Answer
Rot vs pollution? Rot: decay with length. Pollution: particular stale or wrong content that misleads.
Why is it hard to catch? Nothing errors; quality falls only on long sessions.
The recovery when a session has gone bad? Restart with a clean window: goal, constraints, current question.

The idea

An agent calls a billing API, gets a 500, retries, gets another 500. The third try works. For the next twenty turns the agent avoids that API and tells the user billing data "may be unavailable".

Nothing in the window is corrupt. Two error payloads and the model's guess about the cause are still there, and the model reads history as evidence. Content that was true when written has stopped being relevant, and no validation step looks for that.

It compounds, because every answer becomes input to the next.

Adding more explanation to a window in this state rarely helps: the misleading content is still present, now with more text around it. The remedies are by type. A failed call becomes a one-line note that it failed and recovered. A passage retrieved for an earlier subject is dropped when the subject changes. A raw payload is cleared once used. And when the session is too far gone, begin a new one carrying only the goal, the constraints and the current question.

Each remedy is code acting on a typed item; a generic "trim 20%" cannot tell a failed tool call from a user's constraint.

The trade: cleaning removes noise and risks removing state the task needs; cleaning nothing keeps all the state and lets the noise compound.

How it works

What accumulates, why it hurts and what to do with each kind.

Pollutant Why it hurts Remedy
Failed tool calls and retries the model keeps believing the tool is broken replace with a one-line note: failed, then succeeded
The model's own earlier reasoning a wrong step reads as an established fact keep conclusions, drop the working
Stale retrieved passages related-but-wrong text lowers accuracy scope retrieval to its turn; drop on a change of subject
Old raw tool payloads huge, and almost no value left clear in bulk; keep what was extracted
Finished detours compete with the live task fold into the structured summary
Rule What actually happens
It is a loop Output re-enters as input, so a small error grows with depth. A session can be fine at turn five and unusable at turn forty.
Even one hurts In the Chroma study a single related-but-wrong passage lowered accuracy, and four lowered it further.

Evolution

Lineage:Jul 2023 position effects measured2024 agent loops make windows grow unattendedJul 2025 "context rot" named and measured across 18 modelsSep 2025 server-side clearing of tool results
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): the effect is accepted; the remedies are still partly hand-built.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. Newer models decay more slowly with length. What won't change: a model reads its own history as evidence, so a wrong or stale entry will keep being used until something removes it.
  • Checked on: 18 models in the 2025 study; Anthropic's documentation (Oct 2026) states the effect too.

Code

One typed remedy: collapse a run of failures into a note once the tool has recovered.

def collapse_failures(history):
    out = []
    for m in history:
        failed = m.kind == "tool_result" and m.is_error
        recovered = any(n.kind == "tool_result" and n.tool == m.tool and not n.is_error
                        and n.turn > m.turn for n in history)
        if failed and recovered:
            if not (out and out[-1].kind == "note" and out[-1].tool == m.tool):
                out.append(note(tool=m.tool, text=f"{m.tool} failed earlier and has since succeeded."))
            continue                                   # drop the raw error and the speculation after it
        out.append(m)
    return out

Run it at compaction time, since each change to earlier history rewrites the cached prefix.

Measure it

  • Offline: the golden set replayed at depth: the same question asked at turn 1 and at turn 30 of recorded sessions. The gap is the cost of what accumulated; a cleanup should narrow it.
  • In production: quality by turn depth, repeated calls to a tool with the same arguments.
  • Enforced by: the typed cleanup rules and the budget. Whether the model sets aside what remains is not enforced.

Interview

30-second answer: Two failures. Context rot is the measured decline in accuracy as input grows, found across current models and not uniform. Pollution is sharper: a failed tool call, a stale retrieval or the model's own earlier mistake sits in the window and is treated as established. Neither throws. I handle it per type of content, and I know when to restart with a clean, curated window instead of patching.

Q · Mechanism — What is actually in the window that causes this? Four things, roughly by damage. Failed tool calls and the model's speculation about them, which bias it against the tool long after it recovers. The model's own earlier reasoning: a wrong intermediate step has no marker separating "I concluded" from "I was told". Stale retrievals from an earlier subject, which are related enough to mislead. And finished detours taking space.

Q · Trade-off — Why not prune everything except the current turn? The simpler rung, a clean restart, is right when a session is far gone. As a standing policy it fails, because earlier turns hold state: constraints, decisions, what was already tried. An agent stripped to the current turn re-asks and re-tries. So I clean by type, keep decisions in a pinned summary, and do it in rare, large steps because each one rewrites the cache.

Pitfalls

  • "Irrelevant context is harmless; the model ignores it"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a person skims past what doesn't apply.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the content competes. In the Chroma study even one related-but-wrong passage lowered accuracy, and more lowered it further.
    ↳ Think instead: everything in the window is used a little; remove what shouldn't be.
  • "If the conversation is going badly, add more context to steer it back"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: with a person, clarifying helps.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the misleading content is still there. I learned to restart with only the goal, the constraints and the current question.
    ↳ Think instead: a polluted window is reset, not patched.
  • Not the same: context rot vs overflow
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are blamed on "too much context".
    ↳ Difference: overflow is an error with a message. Rot is a quality curve with no error at all, and it starts far below the limit.
    ↳ Think instead: if nothing failed and answers got worse with depth, it is rot.
  • Don't build a cleanup pipeline before measuring by turn depth.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the remedies are known, so applying them all seems safe.
    ↳ What goes wrong: without the measurement you cannot tell whether the cleanup helped, hurt or did nothing.
    ↳ Do instead: split the eval by turn depth first, then add one remedy at a time.
  • Shelf life: "history is read as evidence" and typed remedies are durable. How fast a given model decays with length is not.

Connections

Path:conversation historycontext rotcontext compressionlong-context prompting
  • Builds on conversation history: the tiers that keep most of this out.
  • Contrasts with lost in the middle: position, as against content and length.
  • Owned elsewhere: context rot (Agentic) covers the same decay over a long agent run with many tools.
  • Measured by long-context prompting: the length sweep.
  • Drilled in worse as the session runs.

notes.title: Multi-Turn Prompt Design — Keep State as an Object, Not as a Transcript to Re-read
notes.html:
References

LangChain: short-term memory · Kostric & Balog 2024: multi-query rewriting for conversational passage retrieval · Chroma 2025: Context Rot · Anthropic Engineering: effective context engineering for AI agents

TL;DR

Multi-turn breaks two things a single-turn prompt assumes. The user's message is no longer self-contained ("what about the second one?"). And state piles up in the transcript, where the model has to work it out again every turn. The design move: keep state in a structured object your code maintains, and render it into the prompt. Components that can't see the history, like a retriever, need the follow-up rewritten as a standalone question.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:user turnrewrite to a standalone question (for retrieval only)retrieve for this turnrender state object + recent turns + the user's own wordsmodelupdate the state object in codenext turn

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why does "what about the second one?" break retrieval? The retriever sees only that string; it matches nothing useful.
Where should per-turn state live? In a structured object your code updates, rendered into the prompt.
Who gets the rewritten question? The retriever only. The model gets the user's actual words.

The idea

A flight-booking assistant needs six details. By turn twelve it has four. On turn thirteen it asks for the departure date again, which the user gave on turn three.

Nothing was truncated. The assistant re-derives "what do I have so far?" from the whole transcript on every turn, and this time it derived it wrong.

Stop asking the model to reconstruct state. Keep a small object, {origin, destination, date, passengers, …}, update it in code after each turn, and put it at the top of what the model reads: "Collected so far: … Still needed: …". The transcript becomes supporting evidence. The object is the truth, and unlike "the model remembered", it can be unit-tested.

The second break is upstream of the model. "What about the second one?" means something to anyone who read the conversation. A retriever did not; it embeds that string and returns whatever is nearest. So a small model call first rewrites the follow-up into a standalone question, and only the retriever sees the rewrite.

The trade: explicit state costs a schema and an update step, and can disagree with the transcript; implicit state is free and is wrong now and then, more often as the conversation deepens.

How it works

What the model is given on turn thirteen.

① STATE    Collected: origin LHR, destination DEL, date 14 Nov ← rendered from the state object
② NEEDED   Still needed: cabin class, return date              ← the model need not work it out
③ RECENT   <turn user>…</turn> <turn assistant>…</turn> ×3     ← verbatim: the task in progress
④ CONTEXT  <doc id="fare-7">{{retrieved_for_this_turn}}</doc>  ← fetched with the rewritten question
⑤ QUESTION <user>{{the user's own words}}</user>               ← never the rewritten version

Regions ① and ② replace twelve turns of transcript to re-read.

Rule What actually happens
Rewrite for the retriever, not for the model The standalone question is built for search and reads stiffly. The model answers the user's real words. The rewriting step is owned by query contextualization in the RAG pillar.
Log the rewrite A rewrite that resolves "it" to the wrong thing fetches the wrong document, and the answer looks fine.
Update state in code An explicit updater writes the object after each turn; the next turn does not re-infer it.

Evolution

Lineage:2023 "send the whole transcript" with chat models2023–24 query rewriting for conversational retrieval2024–25 structured state and graph-based agent state in frameworks
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026).
  • Stronger-model test: partly. Stronger models re-derive state from a transcript more reliably. What won't change: a retriever can't read the conversation, and state you can't inspect can't be tested.

Code

The updater, and the test that implicit state can't have.

REQUIRED = ("origin", "destination", "date", "passengers", "cabin", "return_date")

def update(state: dict, extracted: dict) -> dict:
    return {**state, **{k: v for k, v in extracted.items() if k in REQUIRED and v}}   # never erase a filled slot

def render(state: dict) -> str:
    have = ", ".join(f"{k} {v}" for k, v in state.items())
    need = ", ".join(k for k in REQUIRED if k not in state)
    return f"Collected: {have}\nStill needed: {need}"

s = update({"origin": "LHR", "date": "14 Nov"}, {"destination": "DEL", "date": None})
assert s["date"] == "14 Nov" and "destination" in s            # a real unit test on conversation state
print(render(s))
# → Collected: origin LHR, date 14 Nov, destination DEL
# → Still needed: passengers, cabin, return_date

Run on Python 3.9, it prints those two lines. An empty extraction did not erase the date.

Measure it

  • Offline: recorded conversations replayed to turn 20 and beyond, scoring task completion and repeated questions, against the transcript-only version. Single-turn fixtures cannot show these failures.
  • In production: how often the assistant asks for something already in the state object, and the share of retrieval calls made with a rewritten question.
  • Enforced by: the state updater and its unit tests, and the routing that sends the rewrite only to the retriever.

Interview

30-second answer: Multi-turn breaks two single-turn assumptions. The user's message stops being self-contained, so I rewrite a follow-up into a standalone question before it reaches the retriever. And state accumulates; left implicit in the transcript, the model re-derives it each turn and sometimes gets it wrong. So I keep an explicit state object, updated in code and rendered into the prompt, and treat the transcript as evidence.

Q · Mechanism — Why does retrieval need a rewritten query when the model can see the history? Because the retriever can't. It receives a string and embeds it. "What about the second one?" overlaps with no document, so the nearest neighbours are generic text, and the model then has to reconcile irrelevant passages with the conversation. The damage is one component upstream of the model. A small rewriting call fixes it, and its output goes to retrieval only.

Q · Trade-off — Track state explicitly, or let the model infer it from the transcript? The simpler rung is implicit: send the transcript. For short conversations that is right. Explicit state costs a schema and an update step. It pays when state matters and the conversation is long. The deciding argument is testability. I can assert what the state object holds after a sequence of turns; I can't unit-test "the model remembered".

Pitfalls

  • "Multi-turn just means sending the conversation history"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it works for the first few turns, and the API makes it one line.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: history is the easy part. The hard parts are components that can't see it, state that must be exact, retrieval that must not pile up, and growth.
    ↳ Think instead: the transcript is evidence; state, retrieval and budget are separate designs.
  • "Recall was fine on the eval set, so the index must be the problem"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the retrieval metrics were good.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the eval set was single-turn. In production most questions were follow-ups, embedded word for word, so the retriever did its job on a meaningless input.
    ↳ Think instead: an eval set shaped unlike real traffic hides a whole class of failure.
  • Not the same: the rewritten question vs the user's question
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: they ask for the same thing.
    ↳ Difference: the rewrite is built for a search index. The user's words carry tone and emphasis the answer should respond to.
    ↳ Think instead: the retriever gets the rewrite; the model gets the original.
  • Don't build a state machine for a two-turn exchange.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: explicit state sounds like good engineering everywhere.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you maintain a schema and an updater for a conversation whose whole state fits in one message.
    ↳ Do instead: add explicit state when sessions get long or a wrong inference has a cost.
  • Shelf life: "state as an object" and "the retriever can't read the conversation" are durable. How well a model infers state unaided keeps improving.

Connections

Path:conversation historymulti-turn prompt designquery contextualizationstate management
  • Builds on conversation history: the pinned and recent tiers this state sits beside.
  • Owned elsewhere: query contextualization (RAG) covers the rewriting step; state management (Agentic) covers state in an agent runtime.
  • Used by context rot: per-turn retrieval scope removes one pollutant.
  • Drilled in drift by turn 30.

notes.title: Long-Context Prompting — More Context Helps Until It Doesn't; Find Your Own Cliff
notes.html:
References

Hsieh et al. 2024: RULER · Chroma 2025: Context Rot · Modarressi et al. 2025: NoLiMa · Anthropic: prompting best practices

TL;DR

A large window says how much the model will accept, not how much it uses well. The usable length is shorter, and it depends on the task and the model. Nobody can publish that length for you: sweep the input size on your own task and look for where accuracy starts to fall. Put a whole document in when the answer is a property of the whole document. Otherwise retrieve, generously.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchdesign time
Flow:fixed question setpad the input to 4k, 16k, 64k, 256kadd related-but-wrong passagesscore each sizefind where accuracy fallsbudget below itrepeat on every model change

Recall

Prompt Answer
Advertised vs usable length? Usable is shorter; RULER was built to measure the gap.
Why do needle tests flatter? The question shares words with the needle; no reasoning is needed.
Where is your cliff? Not a published number. Measure it on your task and model.

The idea

A team replaces retrieval with "just send all 400 pages" after seeing a model pass a needle-in-a-haystack test at a million tokens. Simple lookups work. Questions that need two facts from different chapters get worse than they were with retrieval.

The needle test is easier than any real task. It hides one distinctive sentence in filler and asks a question that shares its vocabulary, so the model can succeed by matching words: one target, no rivals, no reasoning. NoLiMa removed the shared words, so the answer needed an inference step, and accuracy fell much faster with length. RULER built harder tasks (several needles, tracing, aggregation) and found usable length well below the advertised one. The Chroma study found decline with length across 18 current models, sharper when related-but-wrong passages were present.

So measure your own case. Take a fixed set of questions, pad the context to several sizes, add realistic distractors, and plot accuracy against size. Where the line bends is your working length, and it moves when the model changes.

The trade: a long window buys questions that retrieval can't pose ("is anything in this document inconsistent?") at the price of cost, latency and decay with length on everything else.

How it works

Choosing how to give the model a large body of text.

Approach Good at Breaks when Cost shape
Whole document in the window reasoning about the document as a whole it outgrows the window; accuracy decays with length full input price per question, unless the document is cached
Retrieval, few chunks fact lookup with a source; huge corpora the question needs a global view cheap and fast
Retrieval, many chunks into a large window most production Q&A; eases pressure on retrieval precision past your measured cliff moderate
Per-section calls, then combine "find every instance" and aggregation latency: it is N calls N short calls plus one

When you do send a long input, lay it out as instruction placement describes: documents first, each in a tag with its source, the question last, and ask for the supporting quotes before the answer.

Rule What actually happens
Make the sweep hard One obvious target and no distractors reproduces the needle test's optimism. Add distractors, an inference step and several targets.
The cliff belongs to the model Re-run the sweep after every model upgrade; it moves without notice.

Evolution

Lineage:2023 100k windows; needle-in-a-haystack as the headline testApr 2024 RULER: harder synthetic tasksFeb 2025 NoLiMa: no shared wordsJul 2025 decay measured on current models2025–26 million-token windows standard on top models
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): windows keep growing; how to evaluate them is still being worked out.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. Each generation pushes the cliff further out. What won't change: capacity and competence are different numbers, and only a measurement on your task gives the second.

Code

The sweep. It needs a live model, since the model's behaviour is what is measured.

SIZES = (4_000, 16_000, 64_000, 256_000)

def length_sweep(questions, filler, distractors, llm, grade):
    results = {}
    for size in SIZES:
        correct = 0
        for q in questions:                                         # same questions at every size
            ctx = pad(q.evidence, filler, to_tokens=size)           # the evidence is always present
            ctx = insert(ctx, distractors.related_to(q), n=3)       # related-but-wrong passages, as in real data
            correct += grade(llm(f"{ctx}\n<question>{q.text}</question>"), q.answer)
        results[size] = correct / len(questions)
    return results                                                  # plot it; budget below the bend
# look for: the size at which accuracy starts to fall
# naive belief predicts: flat up to the advertised window

Measure it

  • Offline: accuracy at each input size from the sweep, with and without distractors, per model. The largest size before the fall is the working length that window budgeting uses.
  • In production: answer quality bucketed by input tokens. A downward slope inside the range you serve means the budget is too generous.
  • Enforced by: the budget set from the sweep, in the assembler. Nothing enforces good use of a long input.

Interview

30-second answer: More context helps until it doesn't, and the turning point is well below the advertised window. RULER measures usable length and finds it shorter than claimed; NoLiMa shows needle-in-a-haystack results come from word matching and fall when inference is needed; decay with length shows up across current models. So window size is capacity, not quality. I find my own cliff with a length sweep on my task and design below it.

Q · Mechanism — Everyone passes needle-in-a-haystack now. Why isn't that enough? The task is easier than anything real. It inserts a distinctive sentence into filler and asks a question sharing its vocabulary, so word matching is enough. Remove the shared words, so an inference step is needed, and accuracy falls much more steeply with length.

Q · Trade-off — A million-token window is available. When do you use it instead of retrieval? The simpler rung is retrieval of a few chunks, and for lookup with a source it wins on cost and speed. I use the long window when the corpus fits and the question is about the whole of it: "are there inconsistencies anywhere in this spec?" has no retrieval form. The architecture choice is argued in the RAG decision framework.

Pitfalls

  • "A million-token window means I can put a million tokens in"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the API accepts it without complaint.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: accepted is not used. The length at which realistic tasks still hold is lower, and that is what harder benchmarks were built to show.
    ↳ Think instead: capacity and competence are two different specifications.
  • "Long context makes RAG obsolete"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: if everything fits, selecting looks unnecessary.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it changes retrieval's shape. I expected to delete a component and got to relax its tuning: retrieve more, worry less about precision. Sources, freshness and corpus size still need it.
    ↳ Think instead: a long window makes retrieval easier, not unneeded.
  • Not the same: needle-in-a-haystack vs your task
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "find the answer in a long input".
    ↳ Difference: the needle shares words with the question and has no rivals. Your users' questions rarely share wording with the passage, and similar passages sit nearby.
    ↳ Think instead: trust a sweep with distractors on your own questions.
  • Don't use a long window to avoid building retrieval.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it is less work today.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the corpus outgrows the window, and you build retrieval anyway on a system designed around the opposite assumption.
    ↳ Do instead: decide by the question type and the corpus's growth, not by today's size.
  • Shelf life: "measure your own cliff" is durable. Where the cliff sits, and which benchmark is the current standard, change every year.

Connections

  • Owned elsewhere: context utilization (LLM-Production) covers the benchmarks; the RAG decision framework covers long context against retrieval.
  • Costed in provider prompt caching: what a session-pinned document costs after the first question.
  • Drilled in retrieve again or keep.
